title: Amazon Q2 2026: AWS grows 37%, AI and chip businesses each cross $25B run rate
subtitle: AWS posted its fastest growth in 18 quarters as Amazon's AI services and Trainium chip business each hit $25 billion annualized, and capex jumped 68% to $54 billion.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Amazon reported Q2 2026 revenue of $200.6 billion — the first time the company has cleared $200 billion in a single quarter — up 20% year over year. AWS was the story: $42.2 billion in revenue, 37% growth, the fastest expansion in 18 quarters, and an annualized run rate of $169 billion. CEO Andy Jassy told investors that both the AWS AI services line and the in-house chip business (Trainium plus custom silicon) each cleared a $25 billion annualized run rate, more than doubling year over year. Capital expenditures came in at $54.21 billion, up 68% from a year earlier and roughly $5 billion above consensus. The stock rose more than 9% after the print.

The relevant mechanism is that AWS's AI revenue is finally big enough to change the shape of the cloud market. A year ago, hyperscaler AI revenue was mostly a footnote inside consolidated cloud numbers, and the numbers investors saw were about GPU rental and Bedrock experiments. A $25 billion run rate for AI services alone puts AWS in the same league as Microsoft's Azure AI business — and the parallel $25 billion run rate for Trainium and custom chips is the first concrete evidence that Amazon's non-Nvidia stack is a real revenue line, not a demo.

This lands inside a week where Microsoft reported Azure at a $100 billion run rate on similar AI tailwinds, Meta guided capex sharply higher, and Alphabet booked $82% of cloud growth to AI-adjacent workloads. The full-year hyperscaler capex bill is now tracking above $600 billion for 2026 alone. The pattern is that the three companies with the balance sheets to fund the compute buildout are all reporting the same thing at once: enterprise AI demand is showing up in the numbers, and the constraint on further growth is power, chips, and physical data-center construction rather than customer willingness to pay.

For learners: cloud earnings reports are one of the few reliable ways to see AI adoption without the hype filter, because customers only show up as revenue when they actually pay. When AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud all separately report AI as their fastest-growing segment in the same quarter, that is a stronger signal than any survey or vendor whitepaper. Treat the quarterly hyperscaler prints as the ground truth against which any "AI is stalling" or "AI is exploding" claim should be checked.
